newsitem.title: UK: New SIB chief will to keep eye on UK bank bonuses.
newsitem.headline: New SIB chief will to keep eye on UK bank bonuses.

text.p: The new chairman of Britain's Securities and Investments Board (SIB), Howard Davies, said on Thursday that Britain's new, enlarged financial services watchdog would keep a close eye on banking bonus packages as part of its regulatory role.
"Both the SIB and the Bank of England see pay as a potential risk factor," Davies told Reuters.
"We do not take a view on absolute levels of pay -- that's not for us. What we look at is the way the compensation system affects the behaviour of people in financial institutions."
The question was whether bonuses were encouraging firms to take on more risks than they really wished to, said Davies.
He said he believed regulators should look at bonus systems as one element of the risk framework within an institution.

Davies was speaking following the publication of a report sent to Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown from the SIB's outgoing chairman, Sir Andrew Large, outlining the framework for the new regulatory body, widely dubbed 'super-Sib'.
Under the proposals it will take over responsibility for supervision of the banking industry in the first half of 1998.
The second phase of the plan will also see staff of the self regulatory organisations (SROs) transfer to the new regulator next year.
By the year 2000 the new body will have brought together the regulatory powers of the Bank of England, SIB and the SROs under one roof.

It will have around 2,000 staff, broadly in line with current numbers across the different regulatory bodies and is likely to be based in the City - London's main financial centre - or Docklands on its outskirts.
The process of integrating regulation, including for the first time the supervision and surveillance of banks, was put forward by Brown in May.
The costs of setting up the new body are likely to amount to between five and 10 million pounds ($8.2 million), said Davies.
That compares with the estimated annual cost of financial regulation of around 200 million pounds, he added.
Davies does not expect the annual figure to rise and as is largely the case now, the financial services industry will pick up the bill.
The aim of the new body is to enhance the ability of regulators to act quickly.
The government will decide on whether to give it tougher powers and Davies said he saw a case for making insider trading a civil offence, enabling it to more easily be prosecuted.
"The SIB has quite strong powers but the SROs are between it and market and so the powers are quite difficult to exercise," said Davies.
"Collapsing the two together into one tier improves the ability to act quickly using existing powers. That is more important than the notion of new powers."

The transfer of powers from the Bank of England has been questioned because of the difficulty of coordinating the lender of last resort function, which remains with the Bank, and the supervision function which now goes out to the regulator.
Critics argue that it would be better to keep supervision in the Bank if it has to pick up the pieces when things go wrong.
Davies admitted the argument had some weight but that the advantages of the synergies between supervision of banking and of securities and insurance were greater.

"We can offset the difficulties by an agreement between the regulator and Bank of England which we shall publish in due course explaining how banking failures will be handled." "Broadly the SIB is responsible for the prudential position of individual institutions and the Bank for the assessment of an institutional failure on the market as whole. As long as there is coordination it will work fine." ($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
